summary: Describes how to securely exchange structured business data, such as EDI, XML or other business-to-business data, over SMTP. The data is packaged as MIME content, with authentication and privacy provided by cryptographic means. This is the basis of the AS1 style of exchange.

plainLanguage.summary: Companies send each other orders and invoices. This document says how to put those documents in sealed, signed email envelopes so only the right company can read them.

questions: how to send edi over email securely
what is mime based secure edi
what is a signed receipt in edi
subtitle: How businesses can swap EDI and other data by email with encryption, signatures and signed receipts.

tldr.problem: Companies exchanging orders and invoices over the Internet need privacy, proof of who sent the data, and proof that the other side received it.
tldr.mechanism: The data is wrapped as MIME content, secured with S/MIME or PGP/MIME, and sent over SMTP. The sender can ask for a signed receipt, which is a digitally signed Message Disposition Notification carrying a hash of what was received.
tldr.outcome: A verified signed receipt gives the sender non-repudiation of receipt. Every security feature is optional, so trading partners choose how much to use, and only the full combination of encryption, signature and signed receipt gives the whole set.

today: RFC 3335 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 1767, RFC 1847 and RFC 2298 and its text mentions future Internet-EDI work only as a possibility.

sections.title: Why Secure Business Mail
sections.content:
Earlier work on Internet EDI, RFC 1767, defined MIME content types for Electronic Data Interchange (EDI) data. RFC 3335 adds a full set of security features on top: data privacy, integrity and authenticity, non-repudiation of origin and non-repudiation of receipt.

The document tries to reinvent as little as possible. It names the existing RFCs that, used together, give secure MIME-based EDI (SMTP, message format, MIME security multiparts, PGP and S/MIME, and message disposition notifications) and spells out how they combine and what a user agent must do to comply. Although it focuses on EDI, any other type of business data is also supported, including XML.
sections.plainLanguage: Two shops want to mail each other private paperwork. This memo is the rulebook for sealing it, signing it and getting a signed thank-you note back.

sections.title: The Secure Transmission Loop
sections.content:
The core idea is the secure transmission loop. The sending organization signs and encrypts an EDI interchange using PGP/MIME or S/MIME and asks for a signed receipt. The receiving organization decrypts it and verifies the signature, which confirms the integrity of the data and the authenticity of the sender. It then returns a signed receipt, in the form of a message disposition notification, that contains the hash of the signature from the received message.

The specification does not force all of this. Encryption, signatures and receipts are each optional, which gives eight possible combinations in a trading relationship. Only the last one, encrypted and signed data with a signed receipt requested, offers the whole suite of security features.

The unit of protection is a whole EDI interchange. In ANSI X12 that is everything from segment ISA to IEA, and in EDIFACT everything from UNA or UNB to UNZ. The envelope headers stay encrypted and are not visible in the MIME package. The existing X12.58 and AUTACK security mechanisms are neither required nor forbidden.

For hashing, SHA1 is RECOMMENDED for all outgoing signed messages, and both MD5 and SHA1 should be supported for incoming ones.
sections.plainLanguage: You seal and sign a letter, ask for a signed reply, and the other side opens it, checks your signature and mails back a signed note proving it got exactly what you sent.

sections.title: Structure of a Secure EDI Message
sections.content:
Section 4 lists, for both PGP/MIME and S/MIME, how a message is nested in each of four cases: no encryption and no signature, signature only, encryption only, and both. The EDI payload is always an RFC 1767 content type, application/EDIxxxx or an XML type.

  • Signature only: a multipart/signed (RFC 1847) holding the payload and a detached signature part, which is application/pgp-signature for PGP/MIME or application/pkcs7-signature for S/MIME.
  • Encryption only, PGP/MIME: a multipart/encrypted with an application/pgp-encrypted part containing Version: 1 and an application/octet-stream part holding the encrypted payload.
  • Encryption only, S/MIME: an application/pkcs7-mime body holding the encrypted payload.
  • Both: the signed structure is placed inside the encrypted one, so the signature is encrypted too.

These structures describe only the initial transmission. Receipts are handled separately.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like boxes inside boxes. The paperwork goes in a signed envelope, and that envelope can go inside a locked box before it is mailed.

sections.title: Signed Receipts
sections.content:
A signed receipt is a RFC 2298 message disposition notification (MDN) that the receiver digitally signs as part of a multipart/signed message. The MDN is the first body part and the signature, created over the MDN including its MIME headers, is the second. A receiving agent that supports signed receipts must be able to build a multipart/report with report-type disposition-notification, calculate a message integrity check (MIC) on what it received, and return the signed result.

The sender asks for a receipt with a Disposition-notification-to header holding the return address. To ask for a signed one it adds a Disposition-Notification-Options header with two parameters: signed-receipt-protocol, the signature format (pkcs7-signature or pgp-signature), and signed-receipt-micalg, a preference-ordered list of MIC algorithms (md5, sha1). Both parameters are REQUIRED when requesting a signed receipt, and the recipient should honour the algorithm list from left to right.

The rules are firm. If a signed receipt is explicitly requested, a signed receipt MUST be returned. If the receiver cannot support the requested protocol or MIC algorithms, a signed or unsigned receipt SHOULD be returned. If a signature is not explicitly requested, a receipt may or may not be returned, though an unsigned one is RECOMMENDED at a minimum. A signed receipt MUST be returned even if processing the content failed, and the user must not be allowed to configure the agent to refuse to send one.

The returned MDN carries a Received-content-MIC field, a base64 hash plus the algorithm name, which is set only when the contents were processed successfully. It is computed over the RFC 1767 MIME header and content for signed messages, over the decrypted content for encrypted unsigned messages, and over the content before transfer encoding and without MIME or RFC 822 headers for plain messages.

When the sender verifies the receiver's signature and finds the returned MIC equals the digest of the original message, it has non-repudiation of receipt.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender says, 'please mail back a signed note with a fingerprint of what you got.' If the fingerprint matches, the sender can prove the other side really received it.

sections.title: Dispositions, Errors and Large Messages
sections.content:
An EDI receipt uses the RFC 2298 format with a few profile choices. EDI content is normally handled automatically, so a successful receipt usually carries Disposition: automatic-action/MDN-sent-automatically; processed.

If the receiver cannot honour the signed-receipt request because it does not support the format or the MIC algorithm, it uses the failed type with Failure: unsupported format or Failure: unsupported MIC-algorithms. If it processes the message but something goes wrong, it uses processed with an error modifier. Where partners agree to continue even though the sender could not be authenticated, it uses processed with a warning modifier.

Large interchanges may be split with message/partial. Support for this is OPTIONAL, and it SHOULD NOT be used unless the recipient is known to support it. The receiver must reassemble the original message before sending any MDN, because the MDN describes the whole message.
sections.plainLanguage: The reply note says what happened: all fine, could not unlock it, could not check who sent it, or something else broke. If a package comes in pieces, the receiver waits for every piece before replying.

sections.title: Public Key Certificate Handling
sections.content:
The document takes a practical near-term approach. Partners exchange and certify public keys as part of setting up a trading partnership. The user agent or EDI application must keep a database of the public keys used for encryption or signatures, plus the mapping between each EDI trading partner ID and its RFC 822 email address.

For systems that use X.509 certificates, trading partners are RECOMMENDED to certify each other themselves if they do not use an agreed certification authority. S/MIME users are highly RECOMMENDED to exchange public key certificates as the S/MIME message specification describes. Using a certification authority is OPTIONAL. For the long term, the RFC only says that additional Internet-EDI standards may be developed to simplify setting up partnerships.
sections.plainLanguage: Before trading, two companies swap their special lock-and-signature keys by agreement, like trading phone numbers before you start calling.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The whole document is about secure business-to-business transport, covering privacy and authentication. Its security section quotes guidance from the S/MIME Version 2 specifications.

First, 40-bit encryption is weak and offers little real security over plain text. Using weak cryptography is never recommended unless the only alternative is no cryptography. Strong encryption such as tripleDES or AES is available, and agents should tell users how strong a message's cryptography is when feasible.

Second, certificate processing can fail in many ways: no chain to a trusted CA, a CRL that cannot be checked, is invalid or has expired, an expired certificate or a revoked one. If a certificate is not provably valid and tied to the message, software should take immediate and noticeable steps to inform the end user.
sections.plainLanguage: A weak lock is almost as bad as no lock, and if the software cannot prove a key is genuine, it must tell the person loudly.
